Synopsis:
Wildfires are emerging as a structural power-sector challenge in the U.S., not merely an environmental hazard. Smoke reduces solar irradiance (GHI down 11–17%, DNI down 32–42% near fires), hitting generation precisely during peak summer demand driven by heat waves. This creates a dual pressure: suppressed renewable supply meeting elevated load. Beyond generation losses, smoke and heat degrade transmission line insulating properties, raising flashover and fault risks. Smoke plumes now travel continental distances, affecting regions far from active fires. While annual solar resource impacts remain modest (<5% outside fire zones), the operationally critical risk lies in short-duration, high-intensity smoke events coinciding with demand peaks. The article argues grid operators must treat wildfire smoke as a routine seasonal planning variable alongside clouds, wind, and temperature.

Relevance: IMPLICIT
The article does not mention gas directly, but the logic is implicit: solar suppression + peak demand + transmission stress creates a generation gap that dispatchable fossil fuel capacity (including gas peakers) would be called upon to fill.
Severity score: Spring 10, Summer 35, Fall 10, Winter 5
*(Risk is concentrated in summer; limited cross-seasonal signal; U.S.-centric with no direct European gas market link)*
